name: Made-to-measure suit

card.summary: A suit cut from a standard base pattern and altered to your measurements, giving a closer fit through the shoulders, chest and waist than off-the-rack sizing.

quick.overview:
A made-to-measure suit starts from a tailor's existing base pattern, which is then altered to your measurements and posture. It sits between off-the-rack suits in standard sizes and fully bespoke suits drawn from scratch.

The appearance payoff is fit: sleeves, shoulders, jacket length and waist line that match your proportions make a frame look more deliberate, which is why lifters with large chests and shorter arms in particular discuss custom options.
quick.how: The tailor takes measurements and notes posture, selects the closest pattern, and the buyer chooses fabric and details. A trial garment may be fitted and adjusted, and lead time is up to several weeks. Lifters on forums describe using made-to-measure or alterations to deal with proportions that standard sizes do not cover.
quick.risks: The main downsides are cost relative to off-the-rack, longer lead time, and variable quality between makers, with measurements sometimes taken by intermediaries and sent abroad, as one forum poster described.

lead: A made-to-measure (MTM) suit is a garment built from a standard base pattern that the tailor alters to the customer's measurements. It is distinct from ready-to-wear, which comes in fixed sizes, and from bespoke, which is made from scratch with several fittings [1].

People use MTM to improve how a suit fits and therefore how their body looks in it. Standard sizes assume standard proportions, while a made-to-measure suit can be adjusted for a broad chest and neck, short arms or a trim waist, details that forum members with athletic builds mention [2][3].
No clinical research applies to this topic; the available material is tailoring terminology and forum accounts.

chain: Base pattern altered to those measurements
Jacket and trousers that follow the body's lines
angle.text: A suit that matches your shoulders, chest and waist reads as tailored and can make a physique look more proportioned. Lifters with off-standard proportions cite it as a way around constant alterations.

paras: Made-to-measure sits in the middle of three tiers. Ready-to-wear is mass-produced in standard sizes; MTM adjusts a base pattern to your measurements with a mix of machine and hand sewing; bespoke is cut fresh to specification, traditionally by hand, with multiple fittings and the highest cost [1]. The tailor measures the customer, studies posture, chooses the nearest pattern and alters it, and the customer can pick fabric and details [1].

Strength-training forum members discuss custom suits because lifting changes proportions. One poster said they had short arms and a larger neck and chest and had to amend or custom-order most clothing [3]. Another thread from 2007 describes a user's experience with custom suits from Hong Kong and Bangkok tailors, where measurements are taken locally and sent abroad [2].
